It is God's gracious rescue of humanity through Christ's death and resurrection.
results.response: The gospel, or the Good News of Jesus Christ, is clearly and consistently expressed throughout the New Testament of the Bible. Here are key aspects gathered from the provided passages that define the gospel: 1. **The Power of God for Salvation** (Romans 1:16): - The gospel is the power of God, demonstrating His mighty work in the world and leading to salvation for all who believe, both Jews and Gentiles. 2. **The Message to be Preached** (Mark 16:15, Matthew 24:14, Luke 8:1, 1 Corinthians 15:1): - The gospel is a message that must be proclaimed to all people (the whole creation or whole world), from the time of John the Baptist and Jesus (Luke 16:16) until the end (Matthew 24:14). - This message includes testimony, faith, and standing (1 Corinthians 15:1). 3. **The Central Content of the Gospel** (Luke 8:11, John 6:33): - The parable of the sower (Luke 8:1-15) illustrates how the Word of God (the gospel) is sown in people’s hearts, and the bread of God (the gospel) comes down from heaven, giving life to the world (John 6:33). - Therefore, the gospel centers on the Word of God and the life-giving message it contains. 4. **The Response to the Gospel** (Luke 16:16, Romans 1:16): - People are called to believe the gospel (Romans 1:16), and many force their way into it (Luke 16:16), indicating a willing and enthusiastic response to the message. 5. **The Fruitful Result of the Gospel** (Galatians 5:22): - The gospel produces the fruit of the Spirit in believers’ lives, including love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, and more. 6. **The Community of the Gospel** (2 Corinthians 13:14, 1 Corinthians 1:9): - The gospel brings about the fellowship of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:14), and believers are called into this fellowship with God’s Son, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:9). From these passages, it is evident that the gospel is a message of salvation, centered on the Word of God, which produces transforming results in people’s lives and unites believers in fellowship.

results.question: Does the Bible claim God exists?
results.expected_answer: Yes — Scripture assumes and declares God's existence from its opening line: 'In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth' (Genesis 1:1). Psalm 19:1 says 'the heavens declare the glory of God,' and Romans 1:20 states that God's invisible qualities are clearly seen through creation.
results.response: Yes, the Bible claims that God exists. Here are key passages that affirm God's existence: 1. **Exodus 3:14**: "God said to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM.' And he said, 'Say this to the people of Israel, "I AM has sent me to you."'" - This passage is significant because it reveals God's self-existent nature and his personal name (Yahweh), demonstrating his reality and existence. 2. **Psalm 14:1**: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.' They are corrupt, they do abhorrent deeds; there is none who does good." - This passage directly addresses and rejects the notion of God's nonexistence by stating that such an idea is foolish and corrupt. 3. **Acts 17:29**: "Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man’s device." - Here, the Apostle Paul quotes from a non-canonical source (perhaps Aristotle) to affirm that God truly exists and is not an artifact created by human hands or imagination. 4. **Hebrews 11:6**: "Without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him, for he who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him." - This passage emphasizes the necessity of faith in God's existence as a foundation for a relationship with him. 5. **Revelation 20:11-15**: Throughout this passage, God, the judge, is present and active. It ends by stating, "And if anyone was not found written in the book of life, he was cast into the lake of fire." (Revelation 20:15) - This passage underscores God's reality, power, and sovereignty over human destiny.

results.question: Did Jesus rise from the dead according to the Bible?
results.expected_answer: Yes — all four Gospels record Jesus' bodily resurrection on the third day after his crucifixion (Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24, John 20). 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 lists eyewitnesses to the risen Christ, and Paul calls the resurrection central to the Christian faith: 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is in vain' (1 Corinthians 15:17).
results.response: Yes, according to the Bible, Jesus did rise from the dead. Here are several direct and relevant passages that confirm this: 1. **John 20:1-2, 11-18** - This passage narrates the resurrection of Jesus and His post-resurrection appearances. It describes how Mary Magdalene found the empty tomb and Jesus' risen presence in the garden: - "Now on the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they, and some others with them, were going to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb... she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn't know that it was Jesus... Jesus said to her, 'Don't touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers, and tell them, "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God." ' Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples, '[She said], I have seen the Lord.'" 2. **Mark 16:6-7** - An angel confirms Jesus' resurrection to the women who came to anoint His body: - "But he said to them, 'Don't be amazed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He is risen; he is not here. Behold, the place where they laid him. Go your way, tell his disciples and Peter, "He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you." '" 3. **Luke 24:36-48** - Jesus appears to His disciples in Jerusalem and demonstrates His risen body: - "As they were talking, Jesus himself stood in the middle of them, and said to them, 'Peace be to you.' But they were terrified and filled with fear, and supposed that they had seen a spirit. Jesus said to them, 'Why are you troubled? Why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is truly me. Touch me, and see; for a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.'" These passages affirm that Jesus physically rose from the dead, as described in the Bible, and appeared to many people afterward. Additionally, the overarching theme of the New Testament, as seen in passages like 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, is that Jesus died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, all in fulfillment of Scripture.

results.question: Was Jesus a real historical person according to the Bible?
results.expected_answer: Yes — the Gospels present Jesus as a real historical figure, born in Bethlehem during the reign of specific, datable rulers (Luke 2:1-7), raised in Nazareth, and crucified under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate (Matthew 27:2, 1 Timothy 6:13), events set within verifiable historical context.
results.response: According to the Bible, Jesus Christ was a real historical person. Here are some relevant passages that confirm this: - The New Testament consistently presents Jesus as a historical person: - **Luke 3:23**: "Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began his ministry." This verse explicitly states that Jesus was a real person who began his ministry at a specific age. - **John 1:14**: "The Word became flesh, and lived among us... we saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only from the Father, full of grace and truth." This verse affirmatively declares that Jesus became a human being, lived, and was witnessed by people. - **Acts 1:1-3**: "The first book I wrote, Theophilus, was about all that Jesus began both to do and to teach... until the day in which he was taken up, after he had given commandments through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen." This passage tells of Jesus' ministry and ascension, further reinforcing his historical reality. - Jesus' identity as the Christ (Messiah) is central to the Bible's message, and numerous passages link this to historical events: - **Acts 18:28**: "for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ." This verse indicates that Jesus' status as the Messiah was debated and defended in historical, public contexts. - **1 John 5:1**: "Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God." This verse assumes that the historical belief in Jesus' identity as the Christ was a central component of Christian faith. - Jesus' ministry and teachings were recorded by eyewitnesses and early followers: - **John 21:24-25**: "This is the same disciple who testifies to these things, and who has written these things. We know that his testimony is true. There are also many other things which Jesus did, were his disciples to write them, every one, the world wouldn't have room for the books that would be written." - **Luke 1:1-4**: "Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us—even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us... so also, I, after investigating everything carefully from the beginning, decided to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus." These verses affirm that the Gospels were written by eyewitnesses or based on their accounts. Taken together, these passages make it clear that the Bible presents Jesus not as a mythical or fictional figure, but as a real historical person who lived, taught, was crucified, and resurrection from the dead.

results.question: Why does the Bible say suffering exists if God is good?
results.expected_answer: Scripture traces suffering to humanity's fall into sin (Genesis 3, Romans 5:12), which broke the good world God created. Yet the Bible also teaches that God is present in suffering (Psalm 34:18), can bring good out of it (Romans 8:28, Genesis 50:20), and will ultimately end it (Revelation 21:4). Job wrestles honestly with unexplained suffering without receiving a full philosophical answer, but with an encounter with God himself (Job 38-42).
results.response: The Bible acknowledges suffering's existence as a result of several key reasons, all of which are rooted in the character and purpose of God: 1. **Consequences of Sin (Romans 6:23)**: Suffering and death entered the world because of humanity's sin. "For the wages of sin is death..." God, being good, does not cause or delight in sin, but He does allow its consequences. This is not evidence of God's malevolence but His justice and holiness. 2. **Testing and Growth (James 1:2-4, 1 Peter 1:6-7)**: Suffering can be used by God to test our faith, mature us, and produce endurance, godly character, and hope. "Count it all joy when you fall into various trials, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. And let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking nothing... The testing of your faith develops patience." Even though God allows trials, He is present in them and works through them for our benefit. 3. **The Redemptive Plan of Christ (1 Peter 3:18, 2:24)**: Jesus Christ suffered and died on the cross to redeem humanity from sin and its consequences. His suffering was a necessary part of God's redemptive plan for mankind, demonstrating His love for humanity. "For Christ also suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God, by being put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit." 4. **Persecution for Righteousness (1 Peter 2:20, 3:14, 1 Timothy 4:10)**: Following Christ may lead to suffering, as believers may be persecuted for their faith. However, this suffering is commendable with God, as it proves one's commitment to Christ and trust in the living God. "For it is better, if it is God's will, to suffer for doing well than for doing evil." 5. **Unavoidable Aspect of Life (Matthew 5:45, Psalms 89:10)**: Suffering is a reality in a fallen world, and even the righteous cannot escape it. God does not guarantee a life free from suffering, but He promises to be with His people in their trials (Matthew 28:19-20). He also expects His children to endure suffering as part of their walk with Christ (2 Timothy 3:12). "All men are like grass, and all their glory is like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall..."

results.question: What does the Bible claim about its own reliability?
results.expected_answer: 2 Timothy 3:16 says 'all Scripture is God-breathed' and useful for teaching. 2 Peter 1:21 describes the biblical authors as men who 'spoke from God, being moved by the Holy Spirit.' The Bible presents itself as trustworthy divine revelation, though evaluating manuscript evidence and historical corroboration is a separate scholarly question outside what I can adjudicate as a text-based assistant.
results.response: The Bible claims several key aspects about its own reliability: 1. **Inspiration by God**: The Bible declares that every Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), that is, inspired by God. This means the Bible is not merely a human work, but the very word of God, given to humanity through human authors. > For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. (2 Peter 1:21, KJV) 2. **True and Reliable**: God's word is truth (John 17:17), and God cannot lie (Titus 1:2). Therefore, the Bible is trustworthy and reliable. In 1 John 5:10, it claims that by believing in the testimony given concerning His Son, one can have the testimony in themselves, further emphasizing the reliability of its words. 3. **Life-giving and Transforming**: The word of God is not just true, but it's also life-giving and transforming. It serves as a lamp for our feet and a light for our path (Psalms 119:105), guiding us in our daily lives. In 2 Corinthians 3:18, it's stated that we are transformed by the Spirit of the Lord from glory to glory by the word of God. 4. **Eternal and Unchangeable**: The Bible does not change or become obsolete, but stands firm and eternal. In Matthew 24:35, Jesus declares, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." Similarly, in Isaiah 40:8, it's stated that the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of God stands forever. 5. **Divinely Preserved**: The Bible also claims that it is divinely preserved. For instance, in Psalm 12:6-7, it's stated that God's words are pure words, silver refined in a furnace on the earth, refined seven times. God's words are "kept pure" and have been preserved over generations. These passages collectively underscore the Bible's claim to inspire ultimate trust and confidence in its reliability and power to transform lives.

results.question: What does the Bible teach about how someone is saved?
results.expected_answer: Ephesians 2:8-9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so no one can boast. Romans 10:9 says that confessing Jesus as Lord and believing God raised him from the dead brings salvation. It is God's gift, not something earned.
results.response: The Bible consistently teaches that salvation is a free gift of God, received through faith in Jesus Christ, and not a result of human effort or works. 1. **By Grace through Faith**: Ephesians 2:8-9 makes it clear that salvation is not something we can earn, but rather a gift from God: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no man should boast." This is echoed in Romans 11:6, "And if by grace, then it is no longer by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace." 2. **By Believing in Christ**: Several passages highlight the importance of believing in Jesus Christ for salvation. - John 3:16 states, "For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life." - Acts 16:31 records the jailer's conversion, where Paul and Silas tell him, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household." - Romans 10:9-10 combines belief with confessing Christ's lordship, "That if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart man believes, resulting in righteousness, and with the mouth he confesses, resulting in salvation." 3. **Not by Works**: While good works may follow salvation, they are not the cause of it. Titus 3:5 emphasizes, "Not by works done in righteousness, which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration, and the renewing of the Holy Spirit." 4. **By enduring to the end**: While initial faith is crucial, endurance in that faith is also necessary. Matthew 24:13 warns, "But he who endures to the end will be saved." This enduring faith is a result of God's keeping power, as Phil 1:6 assures, "being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ." 5. **Salvation for all who believe**: The offer of salvation is extended to all people, not just a select group. Acts 15:11 emphasizes, "But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are," indicating that salvation is available to all who believe. In contrast, passages like 1 Samuel 27:11, where David saved people alive, and Isaiah 45:17, "Israel will be saved by Yahweh," refer to temporal, earthly salvation, not eternal salvation, which is the focus of the topic. The Bible is clear that salvation is a gift from God, received through faith in Jesus Christ, and not a result of human effort or works (Ephesians 2:8-9). This message is consistent throughout the New Testament, with variations merely emphasizing different aspects of the faith required (e.g., believing, enduring, confessing). The Old Testament points forward to this gospel message, as seen in passages like Genesis 45:7, where God's plan to save his people is revealed.
